summaries.example: Imagine a friend says, “The library is open.” You can reply, “That is true.” You have not added a new fact; you have agreed with the friend. A deflationist says that many uses of “true” work in this simple way. The word is also useful when we want to say, “Everything the guide says is true,” even when we do not list every sentence.
summaries.summary: Deflationism is a family of views about truth. It says we should not expect to discover a large, hidden property called truth behind every true sentence. Instead, the main clue comes from how the word “true” works. “The statement that snow is white is true” is closely connected with simply saying “Snow is white.” This pattern is called the equivalence schema. Deflationists usually think the pattern tells us most or all of what can importantly be said about truth. They differ about the details. Some say there is no truth property at all; others allow a very thin property that does not explain why different things are true. They also explain why the word “true” matters: it lets us make general statements, such as “Everything the coach said is true,” without naming every sentence. Traditional, or inflationary, theories say more. They try to explain truth as matching facts, fitting together with other beliefs, or meeting another deeper condition. The entry examines different kinds of deflationism and objections about explanation, meaning, rules for asserting beliefs, paradoxes, and general statements.
key_ideas: Deflationists disagree with traditional theories that try to explain what truth is deep down.
Saying that a statement is true often amounts to saying the statement itself.
The word “true” is still useful because it lets us make broad claims without repeating every statement.
Deflationists differ about whether truth is a real property, and, if it is, whether it is a thin or unimportant one.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate asks whether some words need a deep explanation or whether their everyday job is enough. It also shows how a small word can make language much more powerful. Learning about deflationism helps us notice the difference between explaining what a word does and explaining what a thing is.

important_terms.definition: A view that says the word “true” does not point to a deep, hidden thing. Its important job is mostly shown by how we use it in speaking and thinking.
A pattern saying: “The statement that p is true if and only if p.” For example: “The statement that snow is white is true if and only if snow is white.”
A sentence that says something about a subject, such as “The library is open.”
A useful word or idea that helps us talk about many statements at once, such as “Everything Maya said is true.”
A view that truth has a deeper nature, such as matching facts, fitting with beliefs, or being supported at the end of careful investigation.

questions_to_think_about: When does saying “That is true” add anything to a conversation?
Why might it be helpful to say “Everything in the book is true” instead of repeating the book?
Is “true” more like “metal,” which describes a kind of thing, or more like a helpful tool?
Can two people agree that a sentence is true while disagreeing about what the sentence means?

summaries.example: Suppose an astronomer says, “Every result in this data set is reliable.” One way to understand this is as a broad claim about many individual results. The truth predicate lets us express that claim without listing each result. A deflationist can say that this expressive role explains why we need “true,” even if truth itself has no deep, common nature. An inflationist may reply that the success of the predictions needs an explanation in terms of truth, not merely a convenient way to summarize many cases.
summaries.summary: Deflationism about truth is not primarily a traditional theory of the nature of a truth property. It is an approach according to which the important facts about truth are captured by the way “true” functions in language and thought. Its central tool is the equivalence schema: ⟨p⟩ is true if and only if p. For a deflationist, this schema may be conceptually basic or may follow directly from the operation of the truth expression; it is not explained by a deeper correspondence or coherence relation. Inflationary theories reverse this order: they treat truth as a substantive property and use its nature to explain why the schema holds. Deflationism contains several versions. Sententialist accounts apply truth to sentences, while propositionalist accounts apply it to propositions. Minimalism retains a predicate and a property but regards the property as thin or non-substantive. Disquotationalism emphasizes the way quotation can be removed in suitable cases. Prosententialism analyzes truth-talk as functioning somewhat like pronouns whose content comes from an antecedent. A major reason for having the truth predicate, on many deflationary accounts, is expressive. It permits generalizations such as “Everything Smith says is true,” which would otherwise require a special way of quantifying over embedded sentences or an unwieldy list. The entry also surveys challenges. Critics ask whether truth has a causal or conceptual explanatory role, whether deflationism can fit truth-conditional theories of meaning, whether it can explain norms of assertion, and whether it can handle correspondence, truth-value gaps, the Liar Paradox, and generalizations about truth. Responses differ among deflationists, and the entry does not treat the disputes as resolved.
key_ideas: The central deflationary thought is that instances of the equivalence schema may exhaust the significant content of truth-talk.
Different deflationists disagree about whether truth applies primarily to sentences, propositions, or neither, and about whether the equivalence is analytic, necessary, or merely material.
The truth predicate has expressive utility: it can simulate quantification over sentence positions and support broad generalizations.

Minimalism accepts a truth predicate and property but treats the property as non-substantive; disquotationalism emphasizes cancellation or replacement; prosententialism rejects a standard subject-predicate analysis.
Critics argue that truth may explain successful action or science, contribute to theories of meaning, express a norm of assertion, or create problems involving paradox and generalization.
The source presents these as active philosophical disputes rather than settled conclusions.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate concerns the connection between language, logic, and metaphysics. It asks whether a concept can be important because of what it lets us say rather than because it names a deep feature of reality. It also clarifies why philosophers distinguish a word’s expressive role from an alleged property’s explanatory role. Those distinctions recur in debates about meaning, science, belief, and logic.

important_terms.definition: A family of views holding that the significant facts about truth are exhausted by the role of “true” and related expressions, rather than by a substantive metaphysical theory.
The schema that a named sentence or proposition is true exactly when the sentence itself holds: ⟨p⟩ is true if and only if p.
A theory that treats truth as having a substantive nature, such as correspondence with facts, coherence, usefulness, or another explanatory basis.
The question of whether truth is a genuine property. Deflationists may deny that it exists or regard it as thin, logical, abundant, or otherwise non-substantive.
A view focused on sentences and quotation, such as “‘Snow is white’ is true if and only if snow is white.”
A view focused on propositions, such as “The proposition that snow is white is true if and only if snow is white.”
The use of “true” to state claims over many possible sentences or propositions, especially where ordinary language cannot directly quantify over sentence positions.
A version of deflationism treating truth expressions as sentence-level devices that inherit content from another statement, rather than as ordinary predicates naming a substantial property.

questions_to_think_about: If “The proposition that p is true” is equivalent to p, does that make deflationism trivial, or does it still leave open whether truth is substantive?
Can a predicate be grammatically useful without expressing a substantial property?
Does “Everything the scientist believes is true” merely abbreviate many claims, or does truth explain why the scientist succeeds?
Can a deflationary view account for the idea that assertions ought to be true?
What should a theory of truth do with sentences that seem neither true nor false, such as liar-like sentences?

summaries.example: A student says, “The cafeteria is serving pizza today.” You could agree by saying, “What she said is true.” That reply seems to repeat her claim rather than describe a mysterious object called truth. But if you say, “Everything on the school website is true,” you are using “true” to cover many statements at once. Deflationists often say this is the important job of the word. A critic may ask whether the word is doing more when accurate information helps students make successful choices.
summaries.summary: Deflationism about truth is a family of philosophical approaches rather than one single theory. Its main idea is that truth does not have the kind of deep, substantial nature assumed by many traditional theories. The key pattern is the equivalence schema: the statement that p is true if and only if p. Thus, “The statement that snow is white is true” is closely connected with “Snow is white.” Deflationists typically treat this pattern as exhausting the significant content of truth-talk, while inflationary theories add an account of what makes the pattern hold. Inflationists may appeal to correspondence with facts, coherence, inquiry, or another substantive basis. Deflationists disagree among themselves. Some focus on sentences and quotation; others focus on propositions, what sentences say. Some, such as minimalists, allow a truth property but describe it as thin rather than explanatory. Disquotational approaches stress the way “true” can be removed in suitable cases. Prosentential approaches treat truth expressions as sentence-level devices that inherit content from another statement. Even if truth adds little content to a simple claim, the word remains useful. It lets us make generalizations such as “Everything the teacher said is true.” Ordinary language does not easily quantify over sentence positions, so the truth predicate helps express what would otherwise require a long list or an unusual logical device. Critics question whether this expressive role is the whole story. They argue that truth may help explain successful behavior or science, connect with theories of meaning, guide assertion and belief, or express a relation between statements and reality. key_ideas: Deflationists think the equivalence between “p is true” and “p” captures the central use of truth.
Traditional theories add an explanation of why the equivalence works; deflationists generally reject the need for that extra explanation.
The truth predicate is useful for making general claims about many statements without listing them one by one.
There are several forms of deflationism, and their differences concern sentences, propositions, meaning, and the kind of equivalence involved.
An important challenge asks whether truth explains successful actions, scientific success, or other facts rather than merely helping us state them.
Other challenges concern meaning, rules for belief and assertion, correspondence with reality, paradoxes, and the ability to derive broad truth claims.
summaries.why_it_matters: Deflationism gives a clear example of a philosophical disagreement about what explanation should look like. One side emphasizes the practical and logical work a word does; another asks whether that work depends on a real feature shared by all truths. Thinking through this issue strengthens careful reasoning about language, evidence, disagreement, and explanation.

important_terms.definition: A general approach saying that truth-talk is mainly understood through the role of “true,” not through a deep account of a special truth-making substance.
The pattern “The statement that p is true exactly when p.” It connects a truth claim with the statement it concerns.
A view saying that truth has a substantial nature that explains why true statements are true, for example by matching facts.
A property is a feature something has. Deflationists disagree about whether truth is a property at all, and whether it is substantial if it is one.
A claim that covers many cases at once. “Everything the referee said is true” is a generalization.
A version that treats truth as applying mainly to sentences, often using quotation marks around a sentence.
A version that treats truth as applying mainly to propositions, understood as what sentences say.
A family of views emphasizing that truth expressions can work like sentence-level stand-ins, taking their content from another sentence.

questions_to_think_about: Is “That answer is true” just another way of agreeing with the answer?
Why might a philosopher prefer talking about sentences rather than propositions?
Does a useful shortcut have to stand for a real property?
If a belief leads to success because it is true, can that explanation be replaced by stating what the belief says?
Should a theory of truth explain why broad claims about truth are acceptable, or is the equivalence schema enough?
